Delhi to Install First‑Aid Medical Rooms in All 1,086 Government Schools, Spending ₹48.87 crore annually

30 Oct 2026, 06:31 PM IST · GlobeWire Daily Public Services Desk · Source: navbharattimes.indiatimes.com

4 min read

Key takeawaysGood news for Delhi students – medical rooms to be set up in 1,086 government schools, annual spend ₹48.87 crore – Navbharat Times

Overview

The Delhi government announced a new health‑safety initiative that will place a basic medical room in every one of the city’s 1,086 government schools. A trained health worker – either an Auxiliary Nurse‑Midwife (ANM) or a multi‑purpose health worker – will be stationed at each school to provide immediate first‑aid care for minor injuries, sudden illness, dehydration, and other routine health concerns that arise during school hours.

Scheme Details

  • Scope: All government‑run schools under the Directorate of Education, covering primary, middle and senior secondary levels.
  • Staffing: One trained health worker per school, responsible for wound dressing, administering oral rehydration solution (ORS), and offering a place for students to rest if needed.
  • Facilities: A dedicated room where students can receive basic care. Where a separate room is unavailable, the plan calls for the use of alternative spaces or portable cabins.
  • Exclusions: The medical rooms will not provide diagnostic services, prescription medicines, or doctor‑consulted treatment; they are limited to primary, on‑site first‑aid.
  • Gender‑sensitive Provision: A private, secure area will be set up for female students to manage menstrual hygiene comfortably.
  • Funding: The programme is budgeted at ₹48.87 crore per year.
  • Policy Alignment: The initiative is presented as an implementation of the National Education Policy (NEP) 2020, which emphasizes safe, inclusive school environments.

Implementation Plan

The rollout will be phased:

  1. Phase 1 – Schools with existing spare rooms will have a medical room installed first.
  2. Phase 2 – Remaining schools will receive the service through repurposed spaces or portable cabins (often referred to as “pota cabins”).

The exact timetable for each phase was not disclosed in the announcement.

Expected Benefits

  • Immediate Care: Students who suffer cuts, bruises, fainting spells, or dehydration can receive prompt treatment without leaving campus.
  • Reduced Absenteeism: Quick on‑site care may limit the need for parents to take children home for minor ailments, helping maintain attendance.
  • Parental Confidence: Parents gain assurance that schools are equipped to handle health emergencies, aligning with the Education Minister’s statement that every child deserves a “safe and caring environment.”
  • Support for Adolescent Health: The presence of a health worker also opens the door for counseling on puberty‑related issues, especially for girls during menstruation.

Practical Implications for Students, Parents and Schools

  • Students will have a designated space to receive basic care, potentially reducing the severity of minor injuries.
  • Parents can expect that schools will handle routine health incidents, which may influence school choice for families prioritising safety.
  • School administrators will need to allocate space, coordinate with health‑worker recruitment, and integrate the medical room into daily routines (e.g., maintaining supplies like bandages and ORS).
  • Comparative Context: Similar first‑aid schemes exist in a few Indian states (e.g., Karnataka’s “School Health Programme”), but Delhi’s plan is notable for its city‑wide coverage and dedicated staffing budget.
